claims.text: TypeSafe AI opened early access to Jev, their SystemOne model, in the week before this post (September 2026).
Jev is TypeSafe AI's SystemOne model.
TypeSafe's Jev provides a set of AI primitives that let apps, agents, and workflows make decisions based on context.
Jev's decision-making primitives are confidence scoring, multiple choice, and yes/no (noul) questions.
Jev's decision-making primitives are the perfect complement to agentic work.
In the past, having more infrastructure choices usually meant more complexity and technical debt.
GeoDeploy compares every AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud region that offers managed Kubernetes, picks the best one for each geo, and provisions consistent environments across all three hyperscalers.

GeoDeploy's deployment request takes target geos (with traffic share and data-residency rule: EU-only, US-only, or in-country), a container image and platforms (amd64, arm64, or both), a workload shape (replicas, CPU and memory per pod, egress, storage), and constraints (allowed providers, max number of providers, budget).

In GeoDeploy, the TypeScript app takes in the request, fetches live pricing and does all the math; Jev decides which region wins and which modules to use and never does arithmetic, generates code, or invents region names; Pulumi provisions clusters, registries, workloads, and DNS.
GeoDeploy lists every region with managed Kubernetes and uses great-circle distance as a coverage measure.
GeoDeploy fetches current prices from the AWS Price List API, the Azure Retail Prices API, and the Google Cloud Billing Catalog, normalized into a single quote format.
GeoDeploy's deterministic TypeScript bin-packs pods onto nodes, filters out instance types that don't match the image's architecture, and computes a monthly cost for each candidate.
GeoDeploy assembles a Pulumi program from a curated registry of typed modules: EKS, AKS, or GKE; ECR, ACR, or Artifact Registry; ingress; DNS through Route 53, NS1, or Cloudflare; and observability.
GeoDeploy uses the Pulumi Automation API to run a preview and then an update, with one stack per region.
GeoDeploy will not run provisioning unless cloud credentials pass readiness checks.
Every GeoDeploy run writes a plan.json and plan.md with the full decision record, and a web UI shows the deployment on a live globe.
The link /automation/ points to a Pulumi Automation API page that exists.
Jev returns typed answers with calibrated confidence rather than free text.
Jev's choice() primitive picks one option from a closed list and returns the pick, a probability distribution across all options, and a confidence.
Jev's score() primitive rates something against a rubric you describe; GeoDeploy uses 10 levels.
Jev's noul() primitive answers a yes/no question with a single probability.
Jev only ever selects from closed sets, never writes code or does arithmetic, so a hallucinated region like us-west-9 or made-up Pulumi argument cannot happen by construction.
For each geo, GeoDeploy sends Jev a shortlist of up to 40 priced candidates along with constraints and the image's architecture, in a single call.

GeoDeploy's per-geo Jev call asks for one selection (choice), five quality scores (score: coverage, cost fit, maturity, sprawl risk, architecture consistency), two hard checks (noul: data residency, capacity), and a fallback (choice).
GeoDeploy's packages/decide/src/questions.ts contains a buildStageAQuestions function that imports choice, noul, and score from "@typesafe-ai/sdk".
The rubrics follow TypeSafe's advice to "describe situations, not degrees."

Each of the 10 rubric levels is a concrete scenario, running from "Serves users on a different continent with no nearby presence" up to "In-geo with multiple availability zones, directly in or adjacent to the demand geo's primary population center."
The TypeSafe SDK provides a TypeSafeClient whose systemOne method takes state and questions and returns answers with selection.choice, selection.confidence, residencyOk.noul, and coverage.score.
GeoDeploy's ranking runs on weight profiles: latency-optimized (default), balanced, residency-first, and failure-domain.
Because the weights live in code, GeoDeploy's ranking can be re-tuned without calling Jev again.

GeoDeploy weight profiles: latency-optimized {cost 0.13, coverage 0.48, maturity 0.17, sprawl 0.1, archConsistency 0.12}; balanced {0.25, 0.25, 0.2, 0.12, 0.18}; residency-first {0.12, 0.12, 0.38, 0.23, 0.15}; failure-domain {0.08, 0.17, 0.48, 0.15, 0.12}.
In GeoDeploy's composite score, sprawl risk is subtracted, because every extra cloud provider means more credentials, tooling, and on-call runbooks.
In GeoDeploy, cluster and registry modules follow directly from the provider (AWS always means EKS and ECR), and Jev decides ingress posture, autoscaling posture, and node-pool sizing tier.

GeoDeploy confidence gates: data residency threshold 0.95 (hard reject); region for a new cluster 0.90 (top three candidates flagged for human); region when a stack already exists 0.75 (keep existing region); ingress or autoscaling module 0.85 (use registry default); node-pool sizing tier 0.60 (use bin-packing result); global floor for region pick, residency, or capacity 0.50 (drop AI path for that geo).
GeoDeploy's packages/decide/src/engine.ts contains the residency hard-gate check and a validation that the selection is one of the candidates.
Each AiPathAborted in GeoDeploy carries the full attempt (state, questions, and answers), so rejected answers end up in the audit trail.

If a gate check fails, the API times out or errors, or upstream can't be reached, GeoDeploy switches to a deterministic fallback that compares prices across providers while still enforcing residency and constraint checks.
The `geodeploy explain` command shows why each region won.

When self-driving mode is enabled with `geodeploy monitor`, GeoDeploy periodically checks each deployment's CPU utilization and asks Jev one joint question across all regions with options no-change, scale-up:<geo>, scale-down:<geo>, or shift:<from>-><to>, plus a separate disruption-risk check.
In GeoDeploy's self-driving mode, code, not Jev, computes the node-count changes.

In GeoDeploy's self-driving mode, above 0.85 confidence the resize is applied automatically; between 0.70 and 0.85 it is suggested for human approval; below 0.70 GeoDeploy ignores Jev's pick and falls back to a deterministic per-region rule based on observed utilization.
CPU utilization alone makes a poor autoscaling metric and is usually paired with other signals such as median end-to-end request latency and error rates once a traffic baseline is established.
GeoDeploy is released as open source at github.com/pulumi/devx-geodeploy.
GeoDeploy is open source as of this post ("Open source today").
GeoDeploy prices every AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud region with managed Kubernetes.
Jev picks the best region per geo from a closed list so it cannot hallucinate a region.
GeoDeploy provisions consistent clusters with one Pulumi stack per region.
GeoDeploy scales itself in self-driving mode with a human in the loop when confidence is low.
https://docs.typesafe.ai/introduction is the TypeSafe Jev documentation page.
/docs/iac/automation-api/ is a valid Pulumi Automation API docs page.
